summary: Kia's China-built mid-size electric SUV has become one of Australia's best-selling EVs on the strength of space and familiarity: a 513L boot plus a 67L frunk, a conventional dashboard with real climate buttons, and ride comfort Australian reviewers rate highly over broken suburban roads. The trade-off critics keep returning to is charging and range, because the 400V architecture caps DC fast-charging at 140kW and long-term testers get about 424km from the 470km-claimed GT-Line. Reviewers broadly agree the Air grades are the value pick, and split on whether the $71,770 GT-Line's hard-plastic cabin justifies the money against a Tesla Model Y Long Range.
pros: 513L boot (1714L seats folded) plus a 67L frunk, one of the largest load bays among mid-size EVs and roomier than a Tesla Model Y
Air Long Range claims 555km WLTP for $61,170 before on-roads, undercutting the Model Y Long Range AWD while adding standard equipment
Keeps a separate physical climate-control panel and a conventional dash layout instead of burying HVAC in the touchscreen
Five-star ANCAP rating plus Kia's 7-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 7-year/150,000km battery warranty
CarExpert recorded about 17.0kWh/100km in the Air Standard Range and 18-20kWh/100km in the Earth AWD, better than the WLTP claims
cons: 400V architecture caps DC charging at 140kW, and only about 102kW on the Air Standard Range, so 10-80% takes roughly 38 minutes against about half that in a Kia EV6
CarsGuide's GT-Line long-termer averaged 19.8kWh/100km over 932km for a real 424km against the 470km WLTP claim, and carsales saw 23-25kWh/100km in the Earth AWD
Cabin uses a lot of hard plastic that reviewers call low-rent at $70,000, and the climate display is partly obscured by the steering wheel rim
Lane-keep assist over-reacts on country bends and the speed-limit chime fires constantly, both needing to be switched off at every start-up
Surround-view camera and wireless phone charging are reserved for higher grades rather than standard across the range
